chunks: What registers are. The question: What are registers?
A register is a small piece of storage inside the processor that holds one value, such as a 32-bit number. Registers are the fastest storage in the whole system.
The processor takes the numbers for each operation from registers and puts the answer back into a register. A processor has only a few of them, and each has a purpose or a name.
Picture a mechanic's workbench with 32 numbered trays within arm's reach. An instruction says "add tray 5 and tray 6, put the answer in tray 7".
No searching is needed, because the tray number tells you exactly where to go. Only a few trays fit, since a longer bench means a longer reach for every tool.
The warehouse across the yard is main memory: far bigger, but much slower.
The register only changes on a clock edge when write-enable is high: the edge with WE = 1 captures 0x1 farads, while the later value 0xA0 on D in is ignored because WE has dropped.
Between edges the value is stable, which is exactly what makes registers the "memory" of synchronous logic.
Flip-flop: a circuit that stores one bit and updates it on a clock tick. Register: a group of flip-flops that holds one multi-bit value. A 32-bit register is 32 flip-flops.
Register file: the whole set of registers, plus the wiring to read two and write one at a time. Program counter: a register holding the address of the next instruction.
Spilling: parking a value in memory when the registers are full. Peripheral register: a control or status register for a hardware block, at a fixed address.
A simple RISC-V processor (RV32I) has 32 registers of 32 bits each. That is 32 times 32 equals 1024 bits, or 128 bytes of storage.
The instruction "add register 5 and register 6, put the result in register 7" names three registers.
Each name needs 5 bits to pick one of 32, so the instruction spends 3 times 5 equals 15 bits on them. The processor reads two registers and writes one. That is the whole idea.
"A register is a small, very fast storage element inside the CPU made of flip-flops: an n-bit register is n D flip-flops sharing a clock and write enable.
Registers are the top of the memory hierarchy: the ALU reads operands from them and writes results back in about a cycle.
There are general-purpose registers, plus special ones like the program counter, stack pointer and status flags, and pipeline registers between stages.
They're named in the instruction rather than addressed, so there are only a few.
Peripheral control registers in a microcontroller work the same way but sit at memory-mapped addresses."
